articles.title: Don Lemon's presidential ambitions met with skepticism, amusement from his former CNN colleagues
articles.summary: Don Lemon says there's a 65 to 70% chance he'll launch a White House bid, and CNN staffers have strong reactions to his presidential ambitions.
articles.body: Left-wing podcaster and former CNN host Don Lemon claims to be considering a run for president. Count his former colleagues as skeptical at best. Lemon, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump who started his own show after being fired by CNN in 2023, recently said there is a "65, 70%" chance he’ll launch a White House bid. Lemon, who has no political experience, has said he would make a better president than Trump and talked up his appeal to voters. A CNN staffer knocked Lemon's apparent presidential ambitions. "Doesn’t someone, according to Don Lemon, have to be in their 'prime' to run for president? That would certainly rule Don out," they told Fox News Digital. DON LEMON CLAIMS TRUMP'S MAGA MOVEMENT IS 'CLOSEST THING' TO MODERN NAZI PARTY WITHOUT HOLOCAUST The staffer was referring to the infamous 2023 moment when Lemon found himself in hot water for suggesting then-Republican presidential candidate Nikki Haley was past her "prime" at age 51, enraging female colleagues and sparking public fury. Lemon, who is now 60 and almost six years older than Haley, later apologized for the comments. "I love it. Bring it on," another CNN staffer told Fox News Digital of Lemon's possible bid. "It would be fun if he ran. Little bit less boring than the standard 18-people on-stage process that we’re about to watch unfold," they said. "Although, I doubt he actually does it." Lemon's profile was raised earlier this year when he was slapped with a felony indictment for livestreaming a protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a Minnesota church. He has insisted he was working as a journalist and was not part of the group that harassed churchgoers, but Lemon ramped up his criticism of Trump since the incident. "Don does very much want to have influence and feel his contributions matter. Would seem other ways make more sense because running is merely raising money, which is f---ing miserable, and you can’t get anywhere," Lemon’s former colleague said. "I think political office is probably appealing to him. I think a presidential run is obviously not serious, but he could engage in it as a way to launchpad into another office," they continued. "If Don has the itch, there are ways to scratch it that are more serious. It takes a single-minded focus, and he can’t be a media personality and do it at the same time." EX-CNN ANCHOR DON LEMON AGREES TRUMP PLAYED LIBERAL NETWORK 'LIKE PUPPETS' A third CNN staffer said Lemon has done a good job of remaining "relevant" since being fired. "It’s the most open nomination process in 30+ years for the Dems, I think you gotta take it seriously," the second staffer told Fox News Digital. "I’m not saying he is serious, but I am saying he’s said it enough that I can’t dismiss it." Lemon was fired by then-CNN CEO Chris Licht in 2023 and has since launched his own media company. Lemon's tenure at CNN came to a bumpy end, as he had recently been pushed out of his primetime hosting gig to an ill-fated morning show stint with co-hosts Kaitlan Collins and Poppy Harlow. His squabbles on the show and the flap over his infamous Haley comments sealed his fate. DON LEMON REVEALS HE'S 'TOTALLY SERIOUS' ABOUT CONSIDERING A PRESIDENTIAL RUN He wouldn't be the first CNNer to jump into politics. On-air analyst John Avlon launched a New York congressional bid as a Democrat in 2024 but was ultimately defeated. Lemon suggested earlier this year he didn’t have political ambitions but said people had been asking him to do so, and therefore, he was thinking about it. "I actually think I would be a really good president of the United States," Lemon said on the "Can’t be Censored" podcast. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "For the people to want me. What it would take is if I ran a political campaign, a presidential campaign, I would like to run it, and I don't know if this is realistic or not, without having to beg for money. I would like it to be a voter-citizen-driven campaign for as much as it can be," he continued. "Maybe at some point I might have to take a donation. I would rather not do that." Lemon did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Letitia James’ ‘fair’ Cornell rape probe vow collides with accused aide’s ‘quiet’ exit
articles.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James faces recusal demands in the Cornell 7 case after publicly expressing support for Jane Doe before the probe.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James has pledged a full and fair investigation into the Cornell 7 gang rape allegations, years after she faced accusations that she ignored warnings of sexual misconduct against her former chief of staff and allowed him to "quietly resign" while allegedly keeping his accuser in the dark. The claims stemmed from a 2022 lawsuit filed by James' former deputy press secretary, Sofia Quintanar. A New York judge dismissed the claims against James personally and the Attorney General's Office in February 2025. The decision was upheld by an appellate court in May 2026. Those allegations against James have received new attention after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house associated with Cornell University in October 2024. "Kathy Hochul lost faith in the local DA’s handling of the Cornell sexual assault case. So she picked Letitia James. Did you read Sofia Quintanar’s lawsuit, Governor?" Sam Antar, a fraud investigator based in New York wrote on X. CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS "You’re entitled to question the DA’s handling of Cornell," Antar continued. "We’re entitled to question James’s handling of her own aide and your choice of James to restore public confidence." James is already facing calls to recuse herself from the case after an attorney for one of the defendants pointed to social media posts she made days before her appointment that appeared to take the alleged victim’s side. "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable," James posted on X on Sept. 28. "I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you." Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing accused student Gillio Lopes, filed a court petition on Oct. 7 requesting James to be removed from the case. Miltenberg argued that James' remarks raised concerns about whether she could independently evaluate the evidence and determine whether criminal charges were warranted. "New York Attorney General Letitia James has always taken these matters seriously and followed the facts and the law," a spokesperson for James told Fox News Digital. Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told Fox News Digital that James' public comments could complicate her investigation. "It is problematic for a prosecutor like Tish James to be commenting on a case publicly before the investigation is concluded," Rahmani said. "And the problem is, if you file criminal charges, whether it's through a complaint or a grand jury indictment, that may taint the potential jury pool in a criminal case," he added. Rahmani acknowledged that James likely did not anticipate being appointed when she made the remarks but said defense attorneys could still raise concerns about her involvement. Hochul has defended her decision to appoint James. "I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions," Hochul said during an Oct. 2 news conference. "That's exactly what's going to happen in this case." James also pledged in an Oct. 1 statement that her office would be "guided by the facts and the law." "The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James said. But others, in addition to Antar, say New Yorkers shouldn't move on from the previous allegations raised against James by her former employee. "What about justice for former staffer Sofia Quintanar?" Lattina Brown posted on X. "She spoke out about sexual harassment and NY AG Letitia James had this woman blacklisted in the entire state of NY. The Dems turned their backs on this poor woman. Where is the support for the Hispanic woman?" The litigation centered on James' handling of misconduct allegations involving her longtime chief of staff, Ibrahim Khan, whom Quintanar accused of forcibly kissing her at a Brooklyn political fundraiser in November 2021. INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM In her lawsuit, Quintanar accused James of overlooking warning signs about Khan's conduct and protecting him from the fallout after the accusations surfaced. Her lawsuit claimed Khan was allowed to omit his "unlawful conduct" from his resignation statement and accused James of making "misleading statements" to the press about his whereabouts during the investigation. Quintanar also alleged she was not kept updated on the investigation. The complaint pointed to earlier accusations involving Angel Dubose, a former employee who claimed she was drugged and sexually assaulted at a 2014 holiday party while James served as New York City's public advocate. The lawsuit referenced a 2017 New York Post article linking Khan to the alleged assault. However, the newspaper later removed the report after learning that Dubose could not recall who attacked her and had never identified Khan as the perpetrator, The New York Times reported. James said she referred Dubose's allegations to law enforcement and other agencies after learning of them in 2017. The Manhattan district attorney's office and New York City's Department of Investigation later closed their investigations without filing charges. James described those allegations as "unsubstantiated" in a December 2022 NY1 interview. James' office said it first learned of Quintanar's allegations against Khan on Oct. 2, 2022, directed him to work remotely the following day and hired an outside law firm to investigate on Oct. 4. However, the lawsuit was not dismissed entirely. The appellate court allowed a federal civil rights claim against Khan to proceed and revived retaliation claims against Khan and James' re-election campaign. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The investigation substantiated the allegations against Khan, who resigned in November 2022. Those claims centered on allegations that Khan blocked Quintanar from obtaining a campaign job after she rejected his sexual advances. In May 2026, an appellate court upheld the dismissal of Quintanar's claims against James and the Attorney General's Office, finding that the lawsuit failed to sufficiently show James knew about Khan's alleged misconduct. articles.title: Democrats' fury over Ilhan Omar raid draws stinging GOP reminder about raid from the past: ‘Set the precedent’
articles.summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home, igniting fierce partisan debate over immigration fraud and weaponization.
articles.body: Democratic lawmakers erupted online on Monday after news that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had raided the Washington-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., blasting the development as an effort by President Donald Trump to intimidate a longtime political adversary. "The Trump administration’s raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries," U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., wrote in a statement. The Justice Department confirmed that agents of Homeland Security Investigations, ICE's investigative arm, executed a court-authorized search warrant as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Two sources close to the investigation say the search stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. The Minnesota Democrat has repeatedly denied allegations of immigration fraud and claims that she is in the country unlawfully. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION To Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a fellow member of the progressive group known as the "Squad," the development is a clearly personal one. "Donald Trump has been obsessed with Rep. Omar. He has gone after her repeatedly, causing her severe harm and going after the entire Somali American population," Jayapal said, referencing Trump’s wariness of Somali fraud rings in Minnesota that became a national focus earlier this year. "This is his way of bullying his way back into power. This is what authoritarians do," Jayapal added. Democrats online similarly observed the immigration-related focus of the raid, affirming Omar’s status as a citizen of the U.S. HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ "This raid on Rep. Omar’s home is an outrageous abuse of power by ICE. Rep. Omar has been a U.S. citizen for 26 years. She came to the United States as a child and was legally admitted as a refugee," Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., wrote. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., echoed Lieu. "Ilhan Omar came to America legally as a child refugee fleeing civil war, became a citizen and was elected to Congress. Trump is weaponizing the federal government to silence opposition," Sanders said in a post to X. But Republicans pointed out that the public hasn’t had an opportunity to review the details of Omar’s naturalization paperwork either — something that Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., said she had wanted to see for herself but was blocked from using congressional authority to secure. "I tried to subpoena Ilhan Omar and her brother-husband’s immigration records. Both parties blocked it in Oversight," Mace wrote, referring to the powerful oversight committee, the body of lawmakers charged with ensuring the government lawfully carries out its duties. "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and deported home to Somalia." Omar has faced long-standing political pressure stemming from her previous marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in 2009, a marriage that critics claim was to her biological brother in order to commit immigration fraud. Omar has denied that Elmi is her brother, and no charges related to that marriage have been brought against her. Omar and Elmi divorced in 2017. Additionally, Mace pointed out that accusations of politically motivated investigations mirror the raid on Trump's personal residence in Florida in 2022. "All those who celebrated the raid of Mar-a-Lago don't get to cry over the raid at Ilhan Omar's home. Trump's political enemy raided his home. Democrats set the precedent," she added. Other Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., argued that the moment has highlighted the need to especially scrutinize the citizenship credentials of lawmakers before they arrive in office — calls shared by other fellow members. "If these allegations are true, then it needs to be dealt with legally. But ultimately, this is exactly why myself, members like Kat Cammack and Randy Fine have pushed for there to be a disclosure at least for people to know whether members of Congress are dual citizens," Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., said in an interview with Fox News. Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., agreed. "If Ilhan Omar lied on her immigration paperwork, she should be denaturalized and deported — the same as anyone else. No more special treatment," Fine said. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., didn’t speculate as to why the ICE raid had taken place, but quickly affirmed his view that even lawmakers could be subject to scrutiny. "Nobody is above the law. HSI just executed a search warrant at Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C. home. We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!" Emmer wrote. Notably, U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., as of Tuesday morning, had not issued a statement on the raid on Omar’s residence. Neither had Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Republicans in Congress have investigated Omar in the past, evaluating her net worth and the business ties of her husband, Tim Mynett. "Trump is grossly abusing his power to raid the home of Rep. Omar," Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., a fellow member of the progressive group called the "Squad," said in a post to X on Monday. "He has repeatedly attacked her, Somali Americans and Minnesotans. [Omar] has done nothing to justify a pre-dawn raid ahead of the election. I stand with my sister always." Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., another "Squad" member, agreed in a post of her own. "For years, the Trump admin has launched slanderous attacks against Rep. Omar. This morning, the administration sent federal officials to raid her home. We cannot and will not accept this unprecedented abuse of power," Ocasio-Cortez wrote. OMAR'S NEW LEGISLATION TARGETING ICE SPARKS OUTRAGE WHEN THE INTERNET SEES WHAT'S IN IT: 'UN-AMERICAN' "Trump and his DOJ have a bizarre obsession with tearing down Minnesota, our leaders and our communities. This latest action, even as voting has already started in Minnesota, is a transparent attempt to interfere in our election," Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., said. The raid comes less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. According to the Minnesota secretary of state website, absentee voting by mail and in person began Sept. 18, while the state's new early voting process, which allows voters to cast ballots directly into voting machines, begins Friday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The office of Ilhan Omar did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dem making Senate comeback bid says he wouldn't support a Trump impeachment push

articles.title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
articles.summary: Guilfoyle the allegations of improper conduct are "false" and being ambassador was the "honour of a lifetime".
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has announced.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, had been facing mounting scrutiny after reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration and behaving inappropriately while in Athens.

Trump said she had done a good job, but she will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.

Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself against the "false" claims and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".

Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.

"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.

Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.

In a lengthy post on X, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.

"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".

Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.

A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.

In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."

Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on his behalf before she became ambassador.

Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.

According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.

Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".

Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.

Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with his son Donald Jr, to whom she got engaged in 2018.

That relationship ended in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.

Trump noted on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member. The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign. "She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.

The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.

Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.

For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration sees as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.

She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

articles.title: Katie Zacharia responds after criticism of first White House briefing
articles.summary: The brevity of the appearance, along with Zacharia’s delivery and handling of questions, quickly generated criticism.
articles.body:
Katie Zacharia responded after criticism of her first White House press briefing on Tuesday, telling Newsweek via email that "I am grateful to serve President Trump as Press Secretary, and I will diligently and effectively amplify his successful agenda."

During her debut at the podium, Zacharia announced that the White House had asked U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign.

Yet much of the reaction to Zacharia's debut centered on its brevity. She spent just 14 minutes at the podium and took questions from only three outlets before ending the briefing as President Donald Trump prepared to depart the White House for a campaign trip to Alaska.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator who most recently worked for Trump's social media company, was named press secretary on Friday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt , who left the administration in August to spend more time with her family.

Her first appearance offered an early glimpse of how Zacharia intends to approach the job. She told reporters that her goal was to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people" while describing Trump as "his own best spokesperson."

Speaking to reporters before his trip to Alaska, Trump responded to a question about Zacharia's briefing, saying only, "I thought she was very good."

But the brevity of the appearance, along with Zacharia's delivery and handling of questions, quickly generated criticism from former White House communications officials, journalists and commentators.

Katie Zacharia's 14-Minute White House Briefing

Zacharia began the briefing with prepared remarks highlighting Trump's campaign rallies ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and touting the administration's record on issues including energy, tariffs and immigration.

She took her first question from Breitbart News and said she would continue the "new media" rotation introduced under Leavitt that opened briefing-room access to additional media organizations.

Zacharia also made the biggest news of the briefing when she confirmed that Trump had asked Guilfoyle to resign following allegations of improper conduct.

"She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said.

But after taking questions from only three outlets , including one question about how she plans to balance her family life with the new job, Zacharia brought the briefing to a close as Trump prepared to leave the White House.

"In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there," she said.

Current, Former White House Officials React to Zacharia's Debut

Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, gave Zacharia high praise after her first appearance in front of the press.

He told Newsweek via email: "Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."

However, some criticism also came from within Trump's orbit, according to CNN.

CNN White House reporter Alayna Treene reported that several White House officials and presidential advisers described Zacharia's appearance as "awkward" or "stilted," particularly as she read her opening statement.

Trump has shown a willingness to make quick changes to his White House communications operation. The most notable example came in 2017, when Anthony Scaramucci lasted just 10 days as White House communications director . The White House said at the time that Trump believed comments Scaramucci had made about colleagues were inappropriate for someone in his position.

Treene noted that Trump publicly praised Zacharia after the briefing and that some people she spoke with believed the president would give his new press secretary the benefit of the doubt.

Former Biden White House Communications Director Kate Bedingfield described Zacharia's performance as a "rocky start" during a CNN appearance on Tuesday.

Bedingfield said a press secretary needs to project confidence and demonstrate enough command of administration policy to field questions across a wide range of subjects.

"She wasn't able to do that," Bedingfield said, while acknowledging that it was Zacharia's first day. "To send somebody out to the podium who seems incredibly unprepared, unable to answer five, six, seven, eight questions. I mean, typically these briefings can last as long as 45 minutes, an hour."

Bedingfield called the performance "very unimpressive right out of the gate" but also questioned whether Zacharia had been given sufficient time to prepare after being named to the position only four days earlier.

"It is unusual for a press secretary to come into the job and go straight out to the podium like that," Bedingfield said, calling the position "one of the hardest in the entire administration."

Former Biden White House Press Secretary Jen Psaki offered a more blunt assessment.

"Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit…except it wasnt…will have a lot more to say at 9pm," Psaki, now an MS NOW host, wrote on X.

The reactions placed immediate scrutiny on Zacharia as she began a job that requires serving as a public face for the administration and managing the White House operation responsible for responding to reporters.

Bedingfield argued that the latter responsibility could prove just as consequential as Zacharia's televised appearances.

"The press secretary's job is only in part what you see on camera," she said, pointing to running the press shop and overseeing responses to journalists as other major elements of the position.

Former Trump White House Deputy Press Secretary Sarah Matthews, who resigned after the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol, also contrasted Zacharia's debut with predecessors Leavitt and Kayleigh McEnany.

"Love them or hate them: Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt came out swinging in their first press briefings," Matthews wrote on X. "They were sharp, confident, prepared, and proved they had the chops for the job right out of the gate."

She described Zacharia's performance, by comparison, as "a rather underwhelming debut," pointing to the three questions she took and her "heavy reliance on her notes."

"Not exactly in command of the briefing room," Matthews added.

Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who worked under President George W. Bush, offered a more positive assessment, telling Fox News Tuesday that Zacharia benefited from having substantive announcements to make despite the brevity of her debut. He pointed to her disclosure that Trump had added Kentucky to his upcoming travel schedule and her announcement that the administration had asked Guilfoyle to resign.

"There's nothing that makes the job of the White House press secretary easier than delivering hard news, things that nobody knows about, that your job is to reveal it for the first time on behalf of the president," Fleischer said. He added that the announcements "gave her substance" and "gave her something serious to talk about, not just talking points."

Fleischer added: "Talking points are indeed an important part of that job, but making news is even more important."

Experts Critique Katie Zacharia's Performance

Democratic strategist Melissa DeRosa also praised Zacharia's debut during an appearance on Fox News, arguing that the new press secretary avoided becoming the story.

"I thought that she presented well," DeRosa said, adding that Zacharia did not come across as combative as some previous Trump press secretaries.

DeRosa said she initially worried that Zacharia's first appearance could become a "process story," with observers dissecting her delivery rather than focusing on the administration's message. Instead, she argued, Zacharia delivered significant news and quickly left the podium.

"She came out loaded with news and then she dropped the mic and walked away," DeRosa said. "I think from a strategic perspective, that was a really smart move."

Beverly Hallberg, president of District Media Group and a senior fellow at the Independent Women's Forum, also criticized Zacharia's first appearance while acknowledging the difficulty of making a debut at the White House podium.

"There's grace" for it being Zacharia's first day, Hallberg wrote on X, but she argued that White House press secretary "isn't the kind of position where you should be learning on the job."

"You should already be prepared to step into the role, with understandable room to work through the kinks," Hallberg said. "It's completely normal for a press secretary to be nervous during her first appearance, but I'm hoping she'll find her groove because that wasn't a strong start."

Hallberg, who works as a media coach, focused much of her criticism on Zacharia's presentation. She said the new press secretary relied too heavily on her notes, spoke too slowly and appeared visibly nervous. She also criticizing Zacharia's eye contact and tendency to stumble over words.

The debut nevertheless underscored one aspect of Zacharia's philosophy toward the position: She does not intend to compete with Trump for the role of chief messenger.

Zacharia explicitly described the president as "his own best spokesperson," and her decision to end the briefing so reporters could question Trump directly reinforced that approach on her first day behind the lectern.

articles.title: New evidence debunks Talarico psych hospital rumor after ‘mind-numbing malpractice’ fuels firestorm
articles.summary: James Talarico's campaign provided security footage to debunk the Ohio rehab rumor, but critics ask why the evidence wasn't released sooner.
articles.body: A viral rumor claiming Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico secretly spent his recent campaign absence at an Ohio behavioral health center has now been debunked — but new questions are emerging over why evidence that could have quickly undercut the allegation was not made public as the speculation exploded online. The New York Times reported Monday that it reviewed time-stamped security camera images provided by Talarico's campaign showing the Democrat at his Austin home between Oct. 1 and Oct. 8, when his nine-day absence from the campaign trail was fueling mounting speculation about his whereabouts. The images, which the campaign provided to the Times on the condition they not be published for security reasons, offer the clearest independent evidence yet supporting Talarico's account that he was home recovering from the flu and contradict claims that he instead traveled more than 1,000 miles away for treatment at an Ohio behavioral health center. PAXTON’S ESTRANGED WIFE BREAKS SILENCE ON TEXAS SENATE RACE AFTER 'BIBLICAL GROUNDS' DIVORCE But the revelation has also prompted criticism from some observers questioning why Talarico's campaign did not provide similarly verifiable evidence earlier before an unsubstantiated theory about his whereabouts mushroomed across social media and was amplified by prominent conservatives. "In October of an election year, every day and every hour count as candidates do everything they can to meet with voters. So, if you are out of commission for any extent of time, it's easy for voters to wonder what's going on," GOP strategist Mark Bednar told Fox News Digital. "That being said, if there's a simple explanation like an illness, it's even easier to just prove that outright to voters. If the flu was really the case with Talarico, it's mind-numbing malpractice that his campaign didn't quickly and easily demonstrate that." Washington Free Beacon investigative reporter Chuck Ross pointed to the Times report Monday, writing on X that the footage "could have been released a week ago and quashed the rumors." FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON Talarico's campaign had maintained throughout his absence that he was recovering from the flu, and Talarico appeared virtually at an event Sept. 30 while visibly ill and told attendees he had come down with the illness. But his extended absence from in-person campaigning increasingly became a subject of speculation as Election Day approached. The speculation accelerated after Talarico's campaign reposted footage from a February rally on Oct. 3 without initially identifying it as a months-old video. His campaign told the Times it routinely reposts older social media content. "Let’s be fair here. You’re 20 days out from Election Day, and you’re running for senate in one of the biggest states in the country. Use tech to connect: direct to camera videos, do a livestream. To just go dark is malpractice," Matt Gorman, chief communications officer at Targeted Victory, told Fox News Digital. "You’re running for Senate, not some cubicle dweller." The campaign declined to add to its earlier response. "This is a conspiracy theory that has been proven false. James is excited to be back on the campaign trail after recovering from the flu," campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital Monday. "It's been 87 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans' questions in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do," Ennis said. articles.title: Ilhan Omar's wealth scandal takes a turn just one day after raid of her DC home
articles.summary: Jeanine Pirro says her office is investigating Ilhan Omar's financial disclosures after business valuations tied to her husband surged dramatically.
articles.body: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro revealed Tuesday that her office is investigating Rep. Ilhan Omar's financial disclosures, opening a new chapter in the controversy surrounding the Minnesota Democrat's previously reported multimillion-dollar assets. Speaking on Fox News' "America Reports," Pirro said her office was examining Omar's financial disclosures, which previously showed that the reported value of businesses tied to her husband, Tim Mynett, had surged from as much as $51,000 in 2023 to as much as $30 million in 2024. The latest development comes one day after federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home as part of an ongoing criminal investigation involving her immigration paperwork, two sources familiar with the probe told Fox News Digital. The Justice Department confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant Monday as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. It remains unclear whether the search is connected in any way to the financial disclosure investigation described by Pirro. WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION The disclosures drew scrutiny from congressional Republicans, including House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., who requested financial records from two companies tied to Mynett in February. The original filings, examined by Fox News Digital earlier this year, showed millions of dollars in newly reported assets associated with two of Mynett's business ventures — a California-based winery and a Washington, D.C.-based venture capital firm. ILHAN OMAR NOT OUT OF THE WOODS DESPITE FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE REVISION, TOP REPUBLICAN WARNS The winery, eStCru LLC, saw its reported valuation jump from between $15,000 and $50,000 in 2023 to between $1 million and $5 million in 2024. Rose Lake Capital LLC showed an even sharper increase, rising from a reported value of between $1 and $1,000 in 2023 to between $5 million and $25 million the following year. Combined, the businesses had reported values ranging from approximately $15,000 to $51,000 in 2023, compared with between $6 million and $30 million in 2024. Financial disclosure forms report assets in broad ranges rather than exact dollar amounts, meaning the filings did not establish the couple's precise net worth. In February, Comer requested documents and communications related to the finances of eStCru LLC and Rose Lake Capital LLC, raising questions about the dramatic increase in their reported valuations. Omar subsequently amended her financial disclosures in April, reducing the couple's combined reported assets to between $18,004 and $95,000. The revised filing listed her husband's two businesses as having no net value after accounting for liabilities. Omar's office, at the time, said the original disclosures had failed to properly account for liabilities associated with her husband's businesses, creating what it described as a misleading picture of the couple's finances. The congresswoman has repeatedly maintained that she is not a millionaire. MEET THE LONGTIME BIZ PARTNER OF ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND AS QUESTIONS SWIRL OVER HER SKYROCKETING NET WORTH In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct voted 5-1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss misconduct allegations stemming from the financial disclosures. The congressional watchdog found there was not substantial reason to believe Omar had reported false or incomplete information in violation of federal law or House rules. Omar's office characterized the findings as vindication, maintaining that the congresswoman had done nothing wrong. The congressional watchdog's review is separate from the federal investigation described by Pirro on Tuesday. Omar's latest annual financial disclosure, filed in May, listed assets totaling between approximately $20,000 and $125,000, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune analysis. The filing also reported student loan and credit card debt associated with her husband. The Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent target of criticism from President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

articles.title: 'Squad' Democrat formally introduces bill to abolish ICE, Border Patrol and dismantle DHS
articles.summary: The sweeping bill would ban federal border wall funding, close Guantanamo Bay and dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.
articles.body: Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., formally introduced sweeping legislation to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and eliminate Customs and Border Protection (CBP), advancing a radical proposal that would fundamentally overhaul federal immigration enforcement. The progressive "Squad" member's Reimagining Safety Act would replace DHS with a new Department of Community Safety, while preserving several existing federal agencies such as the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). The legislation would eliminate CBP, including Border Patrol, toppling the federal agency responsible for securing America's borders and screening travelers and goods entering the country. 'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT SLAMMED BY TRUMP ADMIN FOR MOST 'RADICAL' PLAN TARGETING ICE YET While certain customs and immigration functions would be transferred to other federal departments under Ramirez's legislation, the proposal would eliminate CBP's existing enforcement structure. The bill's original cosponsors include fellow "Squad" member Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., along with Reps. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., and Jim McGovern, D-Mass., according to Ramirez's office. The legislation would also prohibit federal funding for border walls beginning in fiscal year 2027 and require the closure of the military detention center at Guantánamo Bay within 60 days of enactment. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin previously blasted the proposal in an exclusive statement to Fox News Digital last month. DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE "Radical leftists are calling to defund the police and abolish DHS. It’s NEVER going to happen. Our 270,000 DHS patriots are keeping Americans SAFE— unlike this open-borders politician who refuses to prioritize Americans over illegal aliens," Mullin said. A DHS spokesperson also criticized Ramirez, saying she "should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district — NOT vilifying law enforcement." Ramirez previously defended her proposal in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing the current department should be dismantled and replaced with an agency focused on community safety. 'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING "Every day, Americans wake up with a new reason to dismantle DHS, reimagine safety and build something that honors our shared humanity," Ramirez said. Under the legislation, the TSA and Coast Guard would be transferred to the Department of Transportation, while FEMA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency would move to the proposed "Department of Community Safety." Customs functions would hypothetically move to the Treasury Department, while certain immigration functions would transfer to the Justice Department. None of its proposed changes to immigration enforcement are currently in force. Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar’s embattled husband appears at scene of the HSI raid in midst of criminal fraud investigation
articles.summary: Tim Mynett was spotted outside the D.C. home raided by HSI agents as the criminal fraud investigation into Ilhan Omar's immigration paperwork deepens.
articles.body: The husband of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was captured on camera by Fox News Digital entering their shared Washington, D.C., residence the day after it was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. Tim Mynett, a political consultant, was seen walking down the street with a yellow Labrador dog on a leash Tuesday afternoon before entering the home that was searched early Monday morning amid a federal investigation into Omar's immigration status. His outing came the same day that U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced that her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures connected to reporting of the couple's shared worth. Two sources close to HSI’s investigation say the raid was part of a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME Omar’s husband is at the center of one of the congresswoman's most prominent controversies — her financial disclosure filings decreasing in reported worth significantly within the span of one filing period. Pirro revealed that her office is now investigating Omar's financial disclosures after the Office of Congressional Conduct in September dropped its misconduct investigation into the congresswoman. Tuesday's announcement opens a new chapter of investigations into the Minnesota Democrat. The controversy surrounding Omar’s finances began when a 2024 financial report estimated that Omar and Mynett possessed between $6 million and $30 million in assets, all while the Minnesota fraud scandal within the Somali community was beginning to come to fruition. The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets. His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now. In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0. OMAR DUCKS QUESTIONS AS SCRUTINY GROWS OVER FILINGS THAT SLASHED HER REPORTED WEALTH BY MILLIONS Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities. Mynett was a partner of a firm that worked on Omar’s 2020 re-election campaign. The two announced their marriage in March 2020. This is Omar’s third marriage, but not her most controversial, as the "Squad" Democrat has also come under fire for her first marriage to a man many alleged to be her brother. Critics and skeptics claim the two married as part of an immigration scheme. WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION When White House border czar Tom Homan first announced the "criminal" investigation into Omar, many speculated it would be related to the allegations that she married her brother to evade the United States immigration laws. But a former federal prosecutor recently confirmed to Fox News Digital that statute of limitations would make opening an investigation into the matter difficult. articles.title: Coast Guard firefight puts US, Mexico at odds despite coordinated border operations
articles.summary: A U.S. Coast Guard firefight near the Rio Grande sparked a dispute with Claudia Sheinbaum, who demanded evidence that gunfire came from Mexico.
articles.body: A firefight involving U.S. Coast Guard personnel along the Mexican border has sparked a dispute between Washington and Mexico City over where the gunfire originated, even as the two countries continue coordinating border security operations. The Coast Guard told Fox News Digital that personnel conducting joint interdiction operations near Garceno, Texas, came under fire from the Mexican side of the border Sept. 26 and returned fire. No injuries or damage to Coast Guard vessels or equipment were reported, and the incident remains under investigation. After U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson publicly announced that Coast Guard personnel had come under fire, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum demanded evidence that the shots originated from her country's territory. "We asked for all the evidence ​ because we have no evidence," Sheinbaum told reporters in Mexico City, saying Mexican security forces had not detected shots originating from their territory. MEXICO VOWS US WILL PAY AFTER ICE FATALLY SHOOTS ILLEGAL MIGRANT WHO ALLEGEDLY ATTEMPTED TO RAM AGENT WITH CAR The State Department, however, told Fox News Digital that information about the shooting had been shared with Mexican authorities. "U.S. Coast Guard personnel were fired upon from Mexican territory on September 26, and we have shared the available information with the Government of Mexico through official channels," a State Department spokesman said. The department did not specify what was shared or when, and U.S. officials have not publicly identified the shooters or detailed how they determined the gunfire's origin. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER The incident occurred amid Operation River Wall, a Coast Guard initiative launched in October 2025 to deter illegal migration, drug smuggling and other threats along approximately 300 miles of the Rio Grande. "Over the past year, the Coast Guard has expanded operations in the region, deploying more than 1,000 personnel and more than 30 assets," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital, referring to "Operation Sable". Separately, Mexico's Navy Ministry, led by Secretary Raymundo Morales-Angeles, said 159 "Naval elements", 11 vehicles and two drones were deployed to the Tamaulipas sector. U.S. Northern Command (NORTHCOM) separately told Fox News Digital that American troops are being repositioned to the Rio Grande Valley in anticipation of a seasonal increase in attempted illegal border crossings. Asked whether Mexico had received evidence from U.S. authorities or launched its own investigation, a representative for Mexican Ambassador to the U.S. Roberto Lazzeri Montaño referred Fox News Digital on Monday to Sheinbaum's more recent remarks addressing the incident. Sheinbaum said Mexico's military ministry "maintains" communication with NORTHCOM and the Coast Guard and that a "mirror operation" coordinated with the U.S. remains active. "We want to have a good relationship with the United States within the framework of our sovereignty, our territorial integrity, mutual trust, and coordination without subordination," she said. Her response did not explicitly confirm whether Mexico had received the information Washington says it shared. Fox News Digital also contacted Sheinbaum's office for comment. LATIN AMERICA’S CONSERVATIVE SHIFT FACES ITS BIGGEST TEST YET IN BRAZIL ELECTION Santiago Vidal Calvo, a Venezuelan-born immigration analyst at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital that Sheinbaum's approach to border security is shaped by pressure from Washington and a broader Latin American shift toward right-wing governments. "She has that regional pressure [and] she has the international pressure from the United States" to cooperate on security matters, Calvo said. He suggested Sheinbaum's demand for evidence of the Coast Guard shooting could reflect pressure within her own political coalition to justify working with the Trump administration. "She has a high bar to meet if she wants to ally with the Trump administration internally within her own party and her own government," Calvo said. "We've got to understand this through the lens of what is going on in Latin America. I do think that Sheinbaum's position is substantially different today than it was when Trump got elected," Calvo said. His assessment reflects Sheinbaum's ties to the left-wing Morena Party and the political legacy of her predecessor, former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, commonly known as AMLO. Calvo characterized Sheinbaum as the "last bastion of Latin American socialism," arguing that she could face additional regional pressure if Flávio Bolsonaro defeats President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil's upcoming presidential runoff. Calvo suggested that the rightward shift among South American governments could increase pressure on Sheinbaum to cooperate with Washington on security matters. He said she may face questions about whether "you're the only president of Latin America who's not cooperating with the United States in terms of security?" "Both of those things do lead to a more serious border campaign for both countries," Calvo said. "I have no doubt that the change in South America from left-leaning governments to right-leaning governments has to do with the Trump administration's policy in Latin America," he added. US CHARGES MEXICAN GOVERNOR, TOP OFFICIALS IN CARTEL CONSPIRACY AS MEXICO FIRES BACK OVER PROOF Border security policy analyst Simon Hankinson told Fox News Digital that gunfire near the Rio Grande is not unprecedented, citing accounts he heard during previous visits to the border. Hankinson said cartel involvement was possible but expressed doubt that Mexican military personnel would deliberately fire across the border unless they were acting against orders. articles.title: Trump’s new messenger: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Megan Brand takes stock of the debut of the new White House press secretary. Plus, Natasha Korecki examines whether Republicans may have a surprise opportunity for a breakthrough in the Midwest. — Adam Wollner Trump’s new White House press secretary keeps her first briefing short By Megan Brand President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held an unusually short first briefing with the media today, concluding after less than 15 minutes and calling on just three reporters, all from conservative outlets. Zacharia spent more than half of that time reading remarks before taking questions from Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail. In response to one question, she also revealed that the administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign following allegations of misconduct. Zacharia spent most of her remarks touting the president’s policies and framed her new position as a job to “amplify” the president, something she said she’d done as a conservative commentator. She referred to those appearances, telling reporters that she hopes to “take that into an official capacity.” Now, Zacharia said, she hopes to “only build on, only amplify, and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins” that Trump is “making for Americans, for Americans to understand how much has changed in this brief period of time, what he’s been able to accomplish.” “My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson, and will absolutely be leading the way with that,” she added. Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August, leaving Trump without a chief spokesperson for much of the run-up to the midterms. The president said during a recent rally in Oklahoma that the administration is “not doing a good job of public relations.” At a separate event, he said that the administration was “doing an extremely poor job of promotion,” despite doing an “extremely great job of running the country.” Read more → As Democrats make inroads in red terrain, an unlikely state tightens Analysis by Natasha Korecki Amid the run of rosy storylines for Democrats in this midterm election, one state stands out as a potential outlier: blue-leaning Minnesota. At a time when Senate seats in traditionally Republican states like Texas, Kansas and Alaska appear to be in play for Democrats, Minnesota is surprisingly tight, if recent polls are to be believed. A KARE 11/Minnesota Star Tribune poll released yesterday shows Democrat Peggy Flanagan with a 4-point lead, 47% to 43%, over Republican Michele Tafoya among likely voters in the Senate race. Another 9% said they were still undecided. It’s not the sort of edge one would expect from a state that has gone blue in every presidential election since 1972 or in today’s unfavorable political climate toward Republicans. So what’s different? A few dynamics stand out. First, it’s an open seat, now that Sen. Amy Klobuchar is running for governor. Second, Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and first-time candidate, has attempted to stake out a more independent stance, calling herself a “pro-choice Republican.” There is also the unique set of local issues in Minnesota around alleged fraud related to social services and investigations by the Trump administration. Amid that effort, Democratic Gov. Tim Walz announced he would abandon his political aspirations and not seek re-election. Flanagan, the lieutenant governor, is Walz’s No. 2 in state government. In June, after the Justice Department first announced fraud charges in the state, one poll showed Minnesota voters cited fraud as one of their top issues, and said they blamed Walz and wanted more done to stamp it out. This week, federal authorities searched the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in what sources told NBC News was a federal criminal investigation. In a post on X, Omar called the search “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” adding that over the last decade, President Donald Trump “has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns.” As for the impact on the Senate race, the Democratic super PAC Senate Majority PAC is looking at it through a lens of “Watch what they do, not what they say.” Lauren French, a spokesperson for the group, noted that national Republicans have not put money into the state. And while Senate Majority PAC has paid for some digital ads in Texas, it has not spent in Minnesota, campaign finance records show. “If Republicans really thought this race was competitive, you would see them putting the money that they’re putting into Kansas and South Carolina into Minnesota,” French said. “The fact that they are not is very telling.” Still, National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson Nick Puglia said that the fraud investigations that have happened under Walz’s and Flanagan’s watch “puts Minnesota in play.” “Michele Tafoya is the fighter Minnesotans deserve to stop the fraud and reverse years of failed policies pushed by Flanagan,” Puglia said. articles.body: A Democrat running for county council in eastern Indiana was ridiculed Tuesday after critics claimed she appeared "s--- faced" and slurred her way through attacks on Republicans during a televised candidate forum. During the forum, Fayette County Council candidate Jaime West said she would "fire all Republicans" if elected, railed against "MAGAs" she called "racist" and unintelligent and alleged that a sheriff’s nephew had threatened to kill her. Asked for a final message to voters, West responded: "We have guns too." "This is not a skit," said LibsOfTikTok, a popular conservative punditry account run by commentator Chaya Raichik. "Jaime West, a Democrat running for Fayette County Council in Indiana, gave an embarrassing interview where she appears to mumble and rant the entire time. Is she intoxicated?" Raichik asked on X. LAWMAKER’S STUNNED FACE AND OTHER VIRAL MOMENTS CAP ROUGH WEEK FOR POLITICAL CLASS Former litigator Viva Frei tweeted that the video initially appeared to be a "skit [or] high school video project." "I had to make sure she did not have a neurological disorder that could account for the slurred speech and insane rambling. She doesn’t. And even if she did have a diagnosed neurological disorder, ‘we have guns too’ after talking about firing all Republicans would ordinarily be disqualifying," Frei said. When asked one decision she would make if elected that constituents would find unpopular, West told the moderator, "Fire all Republicans." "I wouldn’t let them — I don’t even talk to them. I don’t like them. They voted against — their own state representative voted against her own party," West continued while also pledging not to raise taxes. DEM SENATE HOPEFULS UNDER SCRUTINY FOR ‘CHOKE THEM OUT’ RHETORIC AFTER TRUMP ATTACK SCARE "Y’all did this to us. … You made this happen. This ICE coming into our communities, stealing people's jobs. "We have guns too," West said as the moderator pivoted to informing viewers about how to vote in the Hoosier State’s elections this year. West could not immediately be reached for comment. While it was not immediately clear which Indiana sheriff West was referring to, Zac Jones, who leads the Fayette County Sheriff's Office where she is running, was stunned by the remark. "I don’t know Jaime West, and she obviously doesn’t know me. I have five nieces and zero nephews. articles.title: Guilfoyle scandal proves too much for Trump with midterms looming
articles.summary: Just days after a series of reports engulfed Kimberly Guilfoyle in scandal, the White House announced and accepted the U.S. ambassador to Greece’s resignation. “We didn’t like what we were reading,” President Trump told reporters after the White House announced the move. The abrupt dismissal marked a stark contrast to how other offenses in the…
articles.body:
Just days after a series of reports engulfed Kimberly Guilfoyle in scandal, the White House announced and accepted the U.S. ambassador to Greece’s resignation.

“We didn’t like what we were reading,” President Trump told reporters after the White House announced the move.

The abrupt dismissal marked a stark contrast to how other offenses in the administration have been handled in Trump’s second term. And even when Trump has dismissed or reassigned top officials following negative press coverage, he rarely makes such a direct link.

Sources said Trump’s handling of the Guilfoyle situation largely came down to timing: Midterm elections are looming, and Republicans are fighting to keep key seats.

“Regardless of whether the allegations are true, you cannot have a story that alleges ‘corruption’ with the midterm elections three weeks away,” one GOP strategist told The Hill.

“When Trump says, ‘I didn’t want to continue reading about this,’ he’s telling the truth; it had become too big a distraction when it’s an all-hands-on-deck moment for the GOP.”

Guilfoyle was the subject of a succession of negative news stories, largely from The Wall Street Journal, laying out a series of embarrassing — and possibly illegal — activity.

Apart from expressing his disapproval of the headlines surrounding Guilfoyle, Trump also distanced himself from his almost daughter-in-law. Guilfoyle was the longtime fiancée of the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., though they broke up well before her appointment to the glitzy diplomatic post.

“No, she wasn’t a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago,” he told reporters Tuesday. “She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading.”

The allegations against her included soliciting $100,000 in cash from a Trump donor to pay down credit card debts before her confirmation hearing and touting her connection to Trump officials, detailed in text messages obtained by The Hill and NewsNation.

The Journal reports also detailed Guilfoyle persistently promoting a Greek shipping firm and including one of its lobbyists in a number of diplomatic meetings, and boasting of close ties with two Greek tycoons who were bankrolling her luxury travel.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told The Hill that the controversy surrounding Guilfoyle only stokes voters’ frustrations with corruption in the administration, pointing out that it is the No. 2 issue they’re focused on in the polls.

A Gallup poll from September found that 89 percent of U.S. respondents said government corruption is widespread. That figure is up 10 percentage points from last year and up 16 percentage points from 2024.

The embarrassing news coverage coincided with Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s diplomatic travel to Greece, where he delivered a sweeping historical speech championing Western civilization with a cinematic backdrop of the Acropolis.

Media reports on the trip largely homed in on getting his reaction to Guilfoyle’s reported conduct. Rubio refused to engage in the questions when speaking to reporters in Athens.

The State Department did not return a request for comment on Guilfoyle’s resignation.

A Republican source close to the Rubio team told The Hill that they think this ouster is different from others in the administration because it occurred under Rubio’s watch. The source described Rubio as a “good actor in all of this.”

“Rubio oversees this department and wants to keep it clean,” the source said, adding that “the corruption issue is growing as a political problem for the Trump admin and this occurred in the weeks leading up to the election.”

“So, you had Marco wanting it and the politics dictating it,” the source continued.

Guilfoyle also adds to the growing list of women fired in Trump’s second administration. The president ousted former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned.

Noem was pushed out shortly after contradicting Trump about his blessing for a government-funded ad campaign, while Chavez-DeRemer was the subject of an inspector general’s probe into a series of abuse-of-office allegations.

By contrast, Mike Waltz, ambassador to the United Nations, was put in his position after taking the fall for inviting The Atlantic’s editor-in-chief into a private Signal chat discussing war plans in Yemen. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was also found to have erred by sharing war plans in the chat.

As Guilfoyle’s conduct emerged in the press, Trump also addressed growing scrutiny around two aides close to his chief of staff Susie Wiles: James Blair and Chris LaCivita.

Trump issued a rare public rebuke against the two men after The New York Times reported they were paid to advise a pro-Russia political party in Republika Srpska, a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

He called the men “outside consultants,” and added that if there’s a conflict of interest, he “will terminate them, immediately!”

Democrats view Guilfoyle’s ousting as only a branch on the poison tree of corruption that is rooted by Trump.

In July, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) launched an “anti-corruption” initiative laying out allegations and concerns over how Trump and his family have enriched themselves alongside connections with foreign governments and favorable federal policies.

“One corrupt Trump official down, hundreds more to go,” Schumer posted on social media Tuesday.

If Democrats seize the majority in the House and Senate in the election next month, expect investigations into the president’s profits while in office and the business dealings of his family and close inner circle.

“When the President himself routinely uses his position to enrich himself and his allies — from crypto schemes to shoddy merch — it is no wonder that cases like this exist,” Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-N.Y.) wrote on social media.

Because of Guilfoyle’s close connections to the Trump family, some have raised the possibility that she might go scorched-earth if fired. However, her resignation message remained supportive of Trump and Rubio.

A former White House official said Guilfoyle might feel motivated to stay on the president’s good side.

“I know a lot of people are imagining she may turn on the family now that they’ve kicked her to the curb. But keep in mind: she probably wants a presidential pardon very badly, and she doesn’t get that if she starts looking to cuddle up to Democrats,” the former official said.

Julia Manchester contributed to this report.

Interior asks court to let it reassess wind approval

The Trump administration is asking a federal court to reassess a prior approval of a nearly-completed offshore wind farm, an escalation of the administration’s attack on wind energy that’s raising questions about an infrastructure deal with Democrats .

On Friday, the Trump administration asked Judge Roy Lamberth to allow it to reassess whether its past approval of the Revolution Wind Project was warranted.

It cited the project’s “potential moderate to major adverse impacts to other uses” of the area off the nation’s coast.

The move is one of a series of attacks the administration has instituted on renewable power and especially wind energy, a particular subject of President Trump’s scorn.

However, this latest action comes as the administration is working on a deal with Democrats that seeks to expedite the buildout of energy and infrastructure projects across the board.

Last month, Senate Democrats and Republicans said they had reached a deal on legislation that seeks to speed the buildout of various types of energy including renewables and fossil fuels by curtailing environmental laws and other provisions.

As the package was being negotiated, the Trump administration’s treatment of renewables was a key point of contention.

When the deal was announced, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said that one outstanding issue was “the question of returning to regular order for wind and solar projects in the Trump administration.”

It’s unclear whether the latest maneuver will impact efforts to get the legislation across the finish line.

White House official Jarrod Agen said in a post on the social platform X that the administration still supports the bipartisan deal.

“This is an old lawsuit brought by the local community—who had serious concerns about this project—against the Biden Administration!” wrote Agen, the executive director of the National Energy Dominance Council.

Rudi Lacatusu, 28, and Mirabela Lacatusu, 26, Romanian nationals accused of targeting victims on Long Island, are now in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody, DHS announced Tuesday. The pair allegedly carried out at least 14 jewelry thefts across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Maryland, according to DHS, which cited local reporting. The stolen necklaces were valued between $2,000 and $3,000 each. A 73-year-old woman was standing outside her Valley Stream, New York, home Oct. 5, when a gold Mitsubishi with a man and woman inside pulled up, Nassau County police said. The female passenger asked how to get to BJ’s Wholesale Club. After the woman helped, the passenger stepped out, asked to hug her and placed two gold-colored necklaces around her neck, according to detectives. A short time later, the woman realized her own gold necklace, worth approximately $2,000, was gone. Investigators linked the suspects to similar thefts in Franklin Square and East Meadow. Each faces three counts of fourth-degree grand larceny, police said. DHS said Nassau County authorities turned the couple over to ICE after their arrests. Kathy Hochul, arguing that sanctuary policies put Americans at risk. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY DHS used the arrests to renew its criticism of New York’s sanctuary policies, calling the state a "hotbed of illegal alien crime" under Hochul. DHS said officers arrested 2,197 illegal immigrants across New York during the operation, including people the department described as murderers, rapists, child predators, drug traffickers and violent assailants. Nassau County police initially issued the suspects appearance tickets directing them to court in Hempstead Oct. 20, according to the department’s arrest announcement. DHS’ statement Tuesday did not specify when ICE took custody of them. The case prompted police to warn residents about distraction scams targeting elderly people, including strangers offering jewelry or gifts, asking to pray together, requesting change or seeking help with a flat tire. articles.body:
Pennsylvania at the center of U.S. measles outbreaks

Pennsylvania recorded its sixth measles-related death on Friday, as the state suffers its worst outbreak of the vaccine-preventable disease in 35 years.

The state has tallied more than 1,100 cases , though experts think that number is likely much higher. The latest death was reported in a 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, according to the county coroner, who attributed the cause of death to “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”

The patient had “a recent history” of having contracted measles, the coroner wrote in a Facebook post, adding that it meets the state health department’s definition of a measles-associated death .

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) has been vocal about blaming Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for a decline in measles vaccinations and distrust in the safety of the shots. The state for months insisted it has the resources to combat the outbreak on its own, and Shapiro in August said he declined Kennedy’s offer of assistance.

Local efforts have been paying off. According to state health department statistics, health center staff have administered more than 5,700 MMR vaccinations at 198 pop-up vaccination clinics in the affected communities since the outbreak began in late April.

Providers have also seen a surge of interest from residents seeking MMR vaccinations. In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer approximately 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine, the state said. In September, they administered more than 56,000 doses .

Pennsylvania health officials said they have been in contact with staff from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention throughout the outbreak and have discussed how best CDC resources could be focused.

The Pennsylvania health department initiated the process to request emergency Epi-Aid — a team of CDC epidemiologists who can provide outbreak-response support — in a September letter to CDC, but only on the condition that the CDC publicly recognize the state’s death count.

The agency to date has only recognized two deaths , but a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that Pennsylvania has formally requested federal aid.

“CDC will deploy additional support to Pennsylvania to work alongside state and local health officials to investigate the outbreak, strengthen response efforts, and prevent further spread,” the spokesperson said.
